name: build-test-review
description: Implement, classify the risk of the change, verify it with an independent QA worker, then an independent fresh-context review whose findings are verified by a second worker before they go back, a blocking security review when the change touches a sensitive surface, a ship-readiness check, and delivery. Round cap 3, then the author steps back; a wrong approach is raised early as change-direction.
when: A task that changes behavior or code in a project, whose requirements are clear enough to implement without a written plan first, and that warrants independent verification and review before delivery. Not for tiny or mechanical work (the chore role, no workflow), not for an unclear or oversized request (plan-build-test-review), and not when no-mistakes is the selected delivery path (delegated-build: it owns review and testing itself).

qa-fix.description: QA failed: the implementer fixes it, then the change is classified and verified again. After three rounds the author steps back instead of taking a fourth.

review-fix.description: Confirmed review, security or ship findings went back: the implementer fixes them, then everything runs again on the new commit. After three rounds the author steps back instead of taking a fourth.

direction.description: A change of direction was raised and the orchestrator chose to reshape: re-plan, at most twice. A reshape starts the QA and review rounds afresh.

implement.instruction: Implement the task. Read the project instructions and its verify convention first. Work in thin verifiable slices, riskiest first. Before you report: run the project cheap checks (tests, build, lint), then run the REAL flow end to end and show what it printed (unit tests alone are not proof). Commit your work to the task branch and report with the result block: base and commit, the evidence (each command and what it printed), what you could not verify, and an answer for every feedback id handed to you (fixed with evidence, or rejected with a concrete reason). If a feedback input is present it is the findings your previous commit was corrected for: address every id, flag the class of bug and fix every instance of it. If the plan or approach cannot meet the acceptance, stop early and end with status change-direction and the evidence instead of finishing a doomed version.

classify.instruction: Classify the risk of the change from the diff itself (the change input, base..head): the tier low, medium or high, whether a security review is required, the sensitive surfaces touched, and the diff-triggered checklist items that match. The author and the task text do not set the tier; the diff does. Read the project REVIEW.md and risk rules from the BASE branch (git show), never from the change; an edit to those rules is itself high risk. Name the one fact the change is safe because of, or write unproven. Record the head commit you classified.

qa.instruction: Verify the change independently against the task acceptance by RUNNING it: the project cheap checks, then the real flow end to end (the project verify convention if it has one), then probes beyond the implementer checks (boundary and error inputs, neighbouring behaviour; property or differential tests where they fit). Scale depth to the recorded risk tier and check only the checklist items whose trigger matches the diff. Rules and gates are read from the BASE branch, never from the change. Never edit the change. Run 1 verifies the whole change; on a re-run (feedback or delta present) first report each handed id (fixed or still failing, with the command that shows it), then verify the delta and re-run what the earlier run covered that the delta could affect. Record the head commit you ran on in the verdict block: a pass is valid only for that commit. If the acceptance itself is wrong or unreachable, end early with CHANGE-DIRECTION.

review.instruction: Review the change in fresh context: correctness first, then maintainability and safety. QA already ran it, so spend attention on what a run does not show. Every finding needs file:line, a concrete failing scenario and the evidence you produced; drop what you cannot demonstrate and anything style-only. Tag severity BLOCKER, IMPORTANT, OPTIONAL (a nit) or PRE-EXISTING (a defect that predates the change: never the author fault) and give the CLASS of bug so every instance is fixed. Run 1 reviews the whole change. Run 2 and later review only the delta (the delta input) plus each previously confirmed finding (fixed or still open), and report a new finding only for a defect the delta introduced or exposed; never repeat a finding listed under posted. If the same class of finding comes back after round 2, the approach is the problem: end with CHANGE-DIRECTION and the evidence. Read rules from the BASE branch. Record the head commit you reviewed.

verify-review.instruction: Try to disprove each finding in the feedback input before it goes back to the implementer. Reproduce each one by running the command or tracing the cited path; vote with up to three independent skeptics for BLOCKER and IMPORTANT findings; keep a finding only if a re-run shows the failure and the failure breaks the stated intent. Drop style-only, intended-behaviour and duplicate findings (merge duplicates by class) and findings that fail to reproduce and are refuted, each with evidence; a defect that predates the change stays as PRE-EXISTING. Every handed id appears exactly once, in feedback (confirmed) or in dropped. You add no findings of your own. Record the head commit.

security.instruction: Security review of the change: threat-model first, then the sensitive-surface checklist (authn and authz, secrets, crypto, parsers and deserialization, injection, path traversal, SSRF, installers and updaters, CI workflow files, dependency and privilege changes, data deletion, network exposure, secret logging). This is a blocking gate: Critical and High map to BLOCKER, Medium to IMPORTANT, Low and Info to OPTIONAL. Cheapest safe proof only; never exploit; redact secrets. Read rules from the BASE branch. Record the head commit you reviewed.

verify-security.instruction: Try to disprove each finding in the feedback input before it goes back to the implementer. Reproduce each one by running the command or tracing the cited path; vote with up to three independent skeptics for BLOCKER and IMPORTANT findings; keep a finding only if a re-run shows the failure and the failure breaks the stated intent. Drop style-only, intended-behaviour and duplicate findings (merge duplicates by class) and findings that fail to reproduce and are refuted, each with evidence; a defect that predates the change stays as PRE-EXISTING. Every handed id appears exactly once, in feedback (confirmed) or in dropped. You add no findings of your own. Record the head commit.

ship.instruction: Decide ship-readiness for the head commit and prepare the delivery package. Check that every recorded gate verdict was for THIS commit (a stale pass is a FAIL); run the project cheap checks again on the head; verify the docs, changelog and version conventions the project requires. Write the PR body: what changed and why; the verification stamp (every command and flow that actually ran, including none where nothing ran, and unchecked items listed as unchecked); the risk tier and the required human approvals (an agent approval never replaces a human one); how to revert (exact command or flag, data effects, time); the non-blocking notes verbatim. A change that is irreversible or hard to reverse is hold-for-human, not ready. Never push, merge or deploy.

deliver.instruction: QA, review and the other gates passed on the head commit. Deliver through the task own delivery mode: for direct-PR the worker that owns the branch pushes it and opens the PR ready for review, with the delivery package of the ship step as the body (Testing = the verification stamp below; Risk; How to revert; the non-blocking notes). Never merge: merging stays with the captain and the configured merge authority, and the human approvals required below are not satisfied by any agent verdict.

redirect.question: A worker, reviewer or the plan reported that the approach itself is wrong (change-direction). Reshape and re-plan, close the task, or escalate?
criteria: reshape: the reported direction is another route to the SAME authorized outcome - no wider scope, no new authority, no extra cost. The reshaped approach goes back in as input; this is not a licence to retry the old approach.
close: the goal is unreachable, no longer worth it, or already satisfied. Closing is cheap - the code was fast to write. Report why.
escalate: the direction changes scope, acceptance, authority, risk or cost, or this is the second reshape: the captain decides.
Never choose reshape to avoid closing, and never grind on a plan the evidence says is wrong. Record the reason; it is kept in the workflow state.

step-back.instruction: The round cap was reached. Do not fix anything and do not start another round. Step back and reconsider the approach itself: from every accumulated finding, name the class of defect that keeps returning and the premise it points at. If the approach is wrong, end with status change-direction and the reshaped approach (or the reason to close the task). If it stands, end with status done and the evidence that the next round would converge; the captain decides whether to grant it. If you cannot decide, end with status blocked.
